historical_record.description: The Beach Chalet holds a group of 1937 Federal Art Project works: Lucien Labaudt's San Francisco Scenes frescoes and monochrome frescoes, a mosaic by Primo Caredio and magnolia-wood carvings of sea creatures by Michael von Meyer. It is City Landmark No. 179.
Built as the Beach Chalet, a municipal restaurant pavilion in a modified Spanish-Moorish manner and the last design of Willis Polk, who died before it was finished.
The restaurant that stood here before the Beach Chalet was a wooden Victorian pavilion known as the Swiss Chalet, put up by the architect W. O. Banks.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 179, Beach Chalet.

Lucien Labaudt — French-born, a fashion-design teacher in the city who had painted the Powell Street fresco in Coit Tower — spent more than two years on the Beach Chalet frescoes, working wet plaster about two square feet a day, painting his friends and family at rest and play around the city so that, as he put it, people without an understanding of art could recognize and enjoy them.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1981.
The City Planning Commission approved, 4-0, a freestanding business sign for the Beach Chalet, finding it in conformity with the General Plan (Motion 14411).
The Art Commission approved Lucien Labaudt's scale drawing for a mural for the Beach Chalet, already accepted by the Park Commission, asking the artist for more information.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved Phase II of the Beach Chalet restoration, paid for by a federal ISTEA grant and the Golden Gate Park bond, to finish what the more than $1 million of 1986 work left undone: ramps into the main portico and to the rear for emergency exit, completed restrooms, and an elevator moved toward the back of the landmark building.
The Recreation and Park Commission awarded M. A. Encinger and Associates a $1,101,639 contract for the Phase II renovation of the Beach Chalet.

The first Beach Chalet, a two-storey building for visitors to the beach, was built for about $8,000, with sitting rooms and an ocean-view balcony upstairs and room for bicycles below. The present building is a later one.
